body.value: Archie's reader drops into any web page as a single <archie-viewer> custom element — no framework, no build step on the host.
Point it at a published library by URL, or at a local .archie.zip to browse exhibits with no internet at all.
Deep-zoom still works inside the embed; tiles stream on demand.
Multiple embeds on one page stay independent — each tag carries its own library.
A pre-baked DZI pyramid streams tiles straight to the canvas; a bare source string auto-detects the right tile handler — IIIF, DZI, or plain image.
Malformed or empty region selectors are skipped safely — a broken box never breaks the read.
Your library is every exhibit you're authoring, gathered in one place. Open one to keep editing, or start a fresh exhibit.
Bind your work to disk however you like — a folder, one portable .archie.zip, or stay browser-only. The current binding shows here and you can switch anytime.
Save status, always visible: Saved, Saving…, or Unsaved. Browser-only work persists in the browser; bind to a file for a copy you can move or back up.
Start an exhibit by bringing in media — images, audio, video, or a IIIF manifest URL.
Open a local image straight from the OS file dialog and annotate it offline — no server, no upload.
An exhibit opens as an overview — its objects laid out as plates on one canvas you pan and zoom, so you see the whole shape before diving into any single image.
Drag plates to arrange them — the layout is yours to compose.
Click any plate to enter its editor and start annotating.
Begin a narrative spine right here — frame these objects into an ordered story.
Pin a note to any region: drag a box on the deep-zoom canvas and the note anchors there. Redraw or nudge the box whenever you like.
Or make a whole-object note with no box at all — a thin colour border frames the entire image instead of a region.
Write the note body in markdown.
Tag it — tags drive filtering and the search finder later.
Assign the note to a reading — one interpretive pass among several.
Delete a note in one click; its mark and region go with it.
Emphasis makes a mark stand out or recede — normal, strong, or muted.
Deep-zoom to pixel detail — but never past native resolution, nor out into an unreadable speck. The camera clamps both ends.
Readings are competing interpretations of the same image — a 'cipher' reading, a 'botanical' reading — each its own coloured pass over the marks.
The rail lists every reading. The eye toggles a reading's marks on or off; the pen picks which reading you're authoring into.
Give each reading a colour — its identity in the legend and on the canvas.
Describe a reading in a line so readers know what lens they're looking through.
Hover a reading to solo it — isolate one interpretation, or compare two side by side.
A narrative is a spine of sections — ordered prose that walks a reader through your objects, one framed view at a time.
Each section points at an object; draw a region and that becomes the camera the reader lands on.
Write the section's prose beside it — markdown, with live cites to other notes.
Reorder sections to retell the story; the reader follows your order.
Annotate sound the way you annotate images — by marking moments on the waveform.
Drag across the waveform to mark a time range; the note anchors to those seconds.
Or drop a point marker at a single instant.
The marker bar shows every annotated moment along the track.
Video gets both axes: pause on a frame, draw a box on it, and the note anchors to that spot at that moment.
Scrub the markbar to jump between annotated frames.
The selector carries time and space together (t=… plus xywh=…), so the mark appears only while that frame is on screen.
Add a map as an object — a basemap you pan and zoom like any image, for notes about places.
Frame a lat/lng extent and anchor a note to that patch of the world.
Basemap tiles stream from an XYZ template as you pan — standard web-map tiling.
Cite another note, object, or exhibit from inside a note — your library cross-links itself.
Or browse thumbnails when you'd rather recognise than recall.
Insert the cite and it renders as a live link — readers hover it for a preview card.
Press Cmd-K and search by text to find what to cite.
Set the exhibit's display title and summary — the name and blurb readers meet first.
Credit the work with an attribution statement.
Choose a license — Creative Commons or RightsStatements.org — so reuse terms travel with the exhibit.
Populate an exhibit with media — drop in images, audio, or video from your machine.
Paste a IIIF manifest URL and Archie pulls in its folios as objects, ready to annotate.
Remote images deep-zoom in place — tiles load with anonymous CORS and a 60-second timeout, no copy required.
Publish turns your exhibit into a static site — shareable, indexable, hostable anywhere.
Choose where it goes: a local folder, a downloadable zip, or straight to GitHub Pages.
For GitHub, give a repo, a branch, and a personal access token; Archie pushes the built pages.
Published pages carry SEO metadata — OpenGraph and Twitter tags, schema.org JSON-LD, a sitemap — so links preview richly and search engines index them.
Each step reports its status — working, done, or the exact error if something fails.
Archie is keyboard-first — a shortcut for every common move, listed in this overlay.
Save, cite (Cmd-K), and dismiss without leaving the keyboard.
Step between objects and open this help from anywhere with a key.
Published exhibits greet visitors as a wall of cards — cover image, title, and how many notes wait inside.
Cards sit in the order you set, so the most important exhibit leads.
One card per exhibit; click through to read.
Long note? Expand it into a centred reading sheet over a dimmed backdrop.
The note list is a sidebar you can drag to resize or collapse; your preference is remembered next time.
Hover a note in the list and its mark solos on the canvas — everything else fades.
Click a mark and the camera fits and highlights it; click a whole-object mark and a thin colour border frames the entire image.
Read an image with its notes pinned right to the regions they describe.
Selecting a note floats its card in beside the canvas; with the sidebar open, the camera centres the mark in the space you can still see.
On touch, scroll the note list without panning the canvas — the two never fight.
Audio and video read with a transcript spine — the words beside the sound, each line a moment you can jump to.
Click a transcript line to seek there; as it plays, the active line highlights and follows along.
The waveform doubles as a map of annotated moments.
Step between sibling tracks from the carousel in a multi-object AV exhibit.
Open at a shared timestamp and the player lands there, paused — no autoplay surprise.
Find anything across the exhibit — open the finder with Cmd-K or just '/'.
Search note text and filter by tag; results update as you type.
Pick a result and the reader jumps straight to that note, whatever mode you're in.
A note can carry its own media — click a thumbnail and it opens full-screen.
Step through a note's images, audio, or video in a carousel with the arrow keys.
The note's text sits beside the media; Esc or the backdrop closes it.
Expand a long note into a centred sheet over a dimmed backdrop — distraction-free reading.
The legend toggles readings: the plain base pass, or the colour-coded interpretations, with a hide-all to declutter entirely.
Hover an in-library cite link and a rich preview card floats in — peek at the cited note without leaving the page.
A narrative exhibit reads as prose beside a canvas — the story on one side, the object it's about on the other.
Click a section and the canvas switches to its object and fits the framed view; the active section lights up in the spine.
Scroll the spine and the canvas follows along.

none: Archie turns images into annotated exhibits — no server, no database, no lock-in. This library holds every exhibit you're building; open one to start.
An exhibit's overview is itself a canvas: drag objects to set their reading order, and the count badge shows how many notes each one carries.
Draw a region, write the note in the popover anchored right where you drew it — the marker follows as you pan and zoom.
The same object, read more than one way: a Reading is a mutually-exclusive interpretive pass, and the legend lets a visitor switch between them.
Sequence sections into a narrative spine — bind prose to an object and a framed region, and the reader's camera follows the story.
Drag across the waveform to mark a time range, or import a VTT/SRT transcript to seed a whole recording's worth of notes at once.
Video adds a spatial dimension: draw a box on a paused frame and set a time window — a combined spatiotemporal selector.
A Map is a fourth medium: regions anchor to true longitude/latitude, so re-framing the basemap keeps them nailed to the Earth.
Cmd+K opens the cite palette — reach any note or exhibit in the library and insert a live, clickable reference.
Set the exhibit's title, rights, and required statement here — the same fields that carry through to the published IIIF manifest.
Drop a folder, paste a IIIF manifest URL, or drag in files directly — the import gate that once required a IIIF server is open.
Publish bakes the whole library into static HTML, JSON, and media — a folder, a zip, or straight to GitHub Pages.
Every action in Studio has a keyboard shortcut — this sheet is always one keystroke away.
Visitors land on the gallery — every published exhibit in the library, one card each.
The reader pairs the deep-zoom canvas with a sidebar of notes; select one and its region solos on the canvas.
A narrative exhibit reads as prose beside a canvas — scroll the spine and the canvas follows, fitting the framed view for each section as you go.
Audio and video play inline with a transcript spine — each line seeks the recording as you read down the page.
The finder searches every note, object, and exhibit in the library at once — press the shortcut and start typing.
A note with an image of its own opens into a full-screen lightbox — the note text stays alongside it.
Long notes expand into a centred reading sheet over a dimmed backdrop — room to actually read, with the Readings legend and citations still in reach.
Drop <archie-viewer> into any page — a read-only Web Component, about half the Studio's bundle, no build step, no unsafe-eval.
